nameStory: Partridgeberry gets its name from the bright red berries that persist through winter, providing food for partridges and other ground-dwelling birds. Early settlers noticed these game birds relying on the nutritious berries during harsh New England winters. The scientific name Mitchella honors Dr. John Mitchell, an 18th-century botanist who studied Virginia plants.
description: Partridgeberry is a tiny evergreen creeper that forms dense mats on the forest floor, rarely growing taller than your thumb. Its trailing stems spread out like a green carpet, decorated with pairs of small, shiny oval leaves and bright red berries. This woodland groundcover stays green year-round, making it a cheerful sight in winter forests. The entire plant hugs the ground so closely you might step over it without noticing.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms flat, creeping mats that trail along the ground, with stems that feel slightly woody but flexible, never growing more than 2 inches tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, dark green and glossy with a waxy feel, staying evergreen with white veins that show clearly against the dark surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pale pink trumpet-shaped flowers appear in pairs during early summer, each with 4 petals that feel papery and have a sweet, delicate fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about the size of a pea persist from late summer through winter, feeling firm and containing several small seeds inside

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender trailing stems root at intervals where they touch the ground, feeling smooth with a reddish tinge, creating interconnected colonies

habitat: Look for partridgeberry carpeting the floor of mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially under oaks, maples, and hemlocks. It thrives in acidic, well-drained soil rich in leaf mold, often growing alongside wintergreen and trailing arbutus. You'll find it from sea level to mountain slopes, preferring partial to deep shade where the forest canopy filters the light.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright green shoot tips, and the evergreen leaves look freshest after winter. Late spring brings the start of flower bud formation.
seasonality.summer: Paired white flowers bloom in early summer, followed by green berries that gradually develop. The glossy leaves are at their most vibrant green.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to bright red and become the most noticeable feature. Leaves may develop slight reddish tinges but remain evergreen.
seasonality.winter: The evergreen leaves and persistent red berries make this one of the few colorful plants visible on the snowy forest floor, creating striking contrast against white snow.

funFact: Each partridgeberry is actually formed by two flowers that fuse together as they develop - if you look closely at a berry, you can still see two tiny dimples on top where the original two flowers joined, like botanical conjoined twins!
confusionNotes: Beginning naturalists sometimes confuse partridgeberry with wintergreen, but wintergreen has alternate leaves (not opposite pairs) and grows more upright. Remember: partridgeberry pairs - both the leaves and flowers come in twos, while wintergreen leaves alternate up the stem like steps on a ladder.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called partridgeberry, these berries are also eaten by many other wildlife including deer, bears, and small mammals. Native Americans traditionally used the leaves to make tea for various medicinal purposes, though the berries are somewhat dry and tasteless to human palates.
compareHints: Partridgeberry is the only Mitchella species in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Among other small trailing plants in the madder family, it's distinguished by its opposite paired leaves and fused twin berries. Unlike other red-berried groundcovers like wintergreen or bunchberry, partridgeberry stays truly flat against the ground and maintains its creeping mat form year-round.
